content.text: Under CSULB's Time, Place and Manner policy, campus kiosks may be used only to promote campus events, activities, or programs sponsored by a Recognized Student Organization or a University-affiliated individual, department, or group. Postings must meet the requirements in Section III.A1 and must also state the event's name, date, time, location, contact information (such as email or website), and the date the material was posted. Each event is limited to 2 flyers (no larger than 8½ x 11 inches) or 1 poster (no larger than 17 x 22 inches) per kiosk. Material can go up no more than 10 business days before the event and must come down within 3 business days after it, although Recognized Student Organizations may post general meeting materials for up to 10 business days during the first four weeks of each semester.

Under PS 11-06, the dean may approve allocating department resources for one or more associate chairs, based on the department's size and complexity. The department chair is responsible for selecting associate chairs, in consultation with the department faculty. Associate chairs perform duties assigned by the department chair, but those duties may not include the chair's role in reappointment, tenure, and promotion (RTP) or in staff evaluations. Serving as associate chair does not entitle anyone to succeed to the department chair position.

The Age Discrimination Act of 1975 is a federal law that prohibits discrimination based on age in any program or activity that receives federal financial assistance, which includes universities like CSULB. As a recipient of federal funds, CSULB may not exclude anyone from, deny them the benefits of, or subject them to discrimination in its educational programs and activities because of age, though the law allows limited exceptions such as age distinctions that are reasonably necessary to a program's normal operation. At CSULB, age is a protected status under the California State University system-wide nondiscrimination policy, and complaints are typically handled through the campus Office of Equity and Diversity (or its Title IX/DHR equivalent). I don't know the exact CSULB policy number, so check with that office or the CSU policy library for the current wording and complaint procedures.

I can't recall the exact wording of CSULB's extension programs policy, so I can't quote its provisions on facilities. Generally, CSU campus policies for self-support extension programs (now run through CSULB's College of Professional and International Education) say these programs may use campus classrooms and facilities. State-supported instruction typically has scheduling priority, and the self-support unit must reimburse the campus for the full cost of the space and services it uses. This reflects the systemwide requirement that state funds not subsidize self-support programs, set out in CSU Executive Order 1099 on special sessions. For the precise language, check the current policy statement on CSULB's Academic Senate or policy website.

I can't quote CSULB's specific signature authority policy verbatim or give its policy number with confidence. Under CSU practice generally, signature authority flows from the Chancellor to the campus President, who delegates it in writing to specific positions or individuals. Any delegation can be **revoked at any time** by the person who granted it, or by a higher authority, and the revocation should be documented in writing. Authority also typically ends automatically when the delegate leaves the position or the university, and the campus's delegation records (often kept by Financial Management or Contracts and Procurement) should be updated promptly. For the exact rules, check CSULB's official policy page or ask the Office of the Vice President for Administration and Finance.

Under CSULB Regulation X, recognized student, faculty, or staff organizations may use information tables to share information about their organization and its activities, provided the tabling does not unreasonably interfere with the campus's instructional program or operations or obstruct pedestrian or vehicular traffic. Each group or organization may hold such events no more than four times a month. Requesters must reserve with the Campus Events Office in PH1-103 at least 3 business days in advance, and same-day reservations are not allowed. Approval is required at least 1 business day in advance.

CSULB generally follows the systemwide California State University "Policy Prohibiting Discrimination, Harassment, Sexual Misconduct, Dating and Domestic Violence, and Stalking," which replaced the older Executive Orders 1096 and 1097. Under that policy, a "complainant" is the person alleged to have experienced prohibited conduct, such as discrimination, harassment, sexual misconduct, or retaliation, whether or not that person files the complaint. Complainants have several rights. These include access to supportive measures, the right to bring an advisor, notice and updates during the process, an opportunity to present information and witnesses, and protection from retaliation. At CSULB, complaints are typically handled through the campus office responsible for equity, diversity, and Title IX compliance, but you should check the current campus and CSU policy pages for exact wording, since these policies are revised periodically.

According to the ASI Bylaws 2025-26, all officers-elected or officers-designated assume their offices and duties on the first day of June or immediately after their appointment and its confirmation by the appropriate authority. The exception is Associate Justices designated under Article VII, Section 1.A.c. Officers filling vacancies by election or succession take office immediately once they meet all the requirements of their respective offices. All officers-elected must also take an Oath of Office upon Senate confirmation, swearing to be guided by the articles and bylaws of the Associated Students, Incorporated, and by integrity and principle so that all students are properly served.

According to the Policy on Complaint Management (https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/policy-on-complaint-management.pdf), all complaints, whether written or oral, are given equal regard and investigated. After acknowledging receipt, the Executive Director assigns the appropriate Division Director to investigate, unless the complaint involves that Director, in which case the Executive Director investigates personally. Within three working days of the assignment, the Director must tell the complainant the timeframe for the investigation and for reporting results, and every attempt is made to finish the investigation and report within 30 calendar days. The investigating Director gets free and unrestricted access to all necessary records and premises, whether owned or rented, though the passage cuts off before listing anything else the Director is provided.

I don't know the specific wording of the CSULB Associated Students, Inc. (ASI) Bylaws for 2025-26 on installation of officers, so I can't quote or summarize that provision reliably. In general, student government bylaws at CSU campuses specify when newly elected officers take office (often at the start of the fiscal or academic year, commonly June 1 or July 1) and may require an oath of office or a formal installation at a designated meeting. For the exact language, check the current bylaws on the ASI website (asi.csulb.edu) or contact the ASI Government office directly.

Under CSULB's PS 11-05 (Discontinuance of Academic Programs), when a request to discontinue an academic program is received, the Vice-President for Academic Affairs must initiate a program discontinuance study (Section 1.400). Section 1.300 allows the study to be skipped, with the request going directly to the appropriate University Councils, if the initiating body presents evidence of at least one listed condition. These conditions are no student enrollment in the previous three years, demand so low that necessary courses haven't been offered in three years, an alternate program in the same unit that better serves students, departed faculty whose replacement the area's long-range planning doesn't support, or an external agency such as a credentialing or accreditation body requiring discontinuance. Even in these cases, a study must still be conducted if any three people (students, faculty members, or administrators) request one.

At CSULB, this provision appears in the campus policy on research misconduct, which follows federal requirements (42 CFR Part 93). When an allegation is not substantiated, the university commits to making all reasonable, practical efforts to restore the respondent's reputation, provided the respondent agrees. Those efforts can include notifying people who knew about or took part in the inquiry or investigation of the outcome, publicizing the final result where the allegation was previously made public, and removing references to the matter from the respondent's personnel file. I can't confirm the exact policy number from memory, so you should check the current text with CSULB's Office of Research and Sponsored Programs or the Academic Senate policy listings.

I'm not certain which "Fund Guidelines" you mean, and I don't know of a specific, widely known document with a section titled "Controlled Games," so I can't explain its exact rules. In funding programs generally, a "controlled games" provision usually defines which projects qualify based on who owns or controls them, such as requiring that the applicant hold the IP or have decision-making authority rather than being a work-for-hire studio. In competitive gaming or chess contexts, "controlled games" can instead mean officially supervised or rated games played under set conditions. If you can tell me which organization or fund publishes these guidelines, or paste the relevant section, I can walk you through what it means.

I can't see the specific Title IX Resources Handbook you're referring to, so I can't say exactly what that section says. An address on W Broadway in Long Beach, CA 90802 (downtown Long Beach) in a Title IX handbook is most likely contact information for an off-campus resource. For example, the Long Beach Police Department headquarters is at 400 W Broadway, and handbooks often list local police as an option for reporting sexual misconduct as a crime, separate from or in addition to a school's Title IX office. If you can share the text around that address, I can explain what that resource does and how it fits into the reporting options.

The passage names "The Age Discrimination Act of 1975" only in its section heading and does not explain what that law requires or how CSULB applies it. The text itself lists other laws the handbook covers, including Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, and other state and federal laws prohibiting discrimination, harassment, sexual misconduct, sexual exploitation, dating violence, domestic violence, stalking, and retaliation. This suggests the Age Discrimination Act is one of several laws referenced in CSULB's Title IX Resources Handbook (https://www.csulb.edu/sites/default/files/2026/documents/OEC%20-%20Title%20IX%20Campus%20Resources%20Booklet_7.%202026.pdf), but the passage gives no further detail about it.

Under the Policy on Discrimation, Harrassment and Retaliation (section 2.2.2), a Complainant initiates the Early Resolution process by contacting the Human Resources Manager. Once the concern is received, the Human Resources Manager will promptly meet with the Complainant to discuss it and, as appropriate, discuss reasonable interim remedies. If the allegation involves Sexual Misconduct, Dating or Domestic Violence, or Stalking, the Complainant will be advised to immediately file a Formal Complaint, because Early Resolution is not appropriate for those allegations.

I can't quote CSULB's specific hazard assessment policy text with confidence, but campus policies like it generally follow Cal/OSHA requirements. Under the Injury and Illness Prevention Program standard (Title 8 CCR §3203), employers must identify and evaluate workplace hazards through periodic inspections and correct them promptly. Under the PPE standard (Title 8 CCR §3380), supervisors must assess work areas for hazards and document a written certification of that assessment to determine the required personal protective equipment. For CSULB's exact procedures, forms, and responsibilities, check the university's Environmental Health & Safety office or its IIPP document.

I can't say for certain which institution's "Policy on Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation" you mean, since many universities and organizations use that title, so I can only describe how early resolution typically works under such policies. Early resolution (sometimes called informal or alternative resolution) is usually initiated when the complainant contacts the designated office, often the equity, civil rights, or Title IX office, and requests it, either before or instead of a formal complaint and investigation. The office then assesses whether the matter is appropriate for that pathway, which often excludes certain serious allegations, and both parties generally must agree voluntarily. Either party can typically withdraw and move to the formal process before an agreement is finalized. For the exact steps, eligibility rules, and timelines, check your institution's version of the policy or contact its equity office directly.

I don't know the specific text or policy number of a CSULB event set-up policy, so I can't quote it accurately. Universities like CSULB generally require events to be registered and approved in advance through the campus event or reservation office. Set-up details such as furniture, audiovisual equipment, staging, and facilities services are usually requested through that office by a set deadline. Organizers typically must also follow fire-code occupancy limits, safety and accessibility requirements, and rules about decorations, food, and clean-up. For the authoritative policy, check CSULB's official website or contact its University Events or Student Union reservations office directly.

In many university and public-institution "Time, Place and Manner" policies, the "Kiosks" section governs designated physical structures, such as freestanding bulletin boards or posting pillars, where people may put up flyers, posters, and other printed notices. These rules usually specify who may post (sometimes anyone, sometimes only registered student organizations or affiliates), the maximum size of materials, how many copies may be posted, and how long items may stay up before removal. They also tend to require sponsor identification, prohibit covering others' materials, and restrict adhesives or methods that damage the kiosk. Because these regulations must be content-neutral, they control how and where materials are posted rather than what they say. The exact details vary by institution, so check the specific policy text for your campus or organization.

Under section 6.2.1 of the Policy on Information Systems, once an investigation confirms a security breach involving notice triggering information, the CSULB Office of Information Security Management and Compliance must notify the Vice President of Administration and Finance and the Office of General Counsel. If the breach is large enough that a press release may be needed, that office also notifies the Senior Director, Information Security Management, the Associate Vice President, University Relations, and the Office of the Chancellor, with a copy to the CIO/Assistant Vice Chancellor. The office then confirms the breach to the responsible department and gives it advice and guidance. It also starts the campus breach notification process, working with the Executive Director or designee responsible for the breached equipment to handle the response and inquiries properly, and guides the employees designated to answer breach notification inquiries.

Under the Policy on Agency Accounts, any revenue generated by activities that are supported fully or partly by ASI fees must be deposited to and administered by the ASI Business Office. If the revenue fulfills a budgetary commitment, it goes into an ASI budget account. Otherwise, it is deposited into the organization's agency account. This provision appears as item 2.3 in the policy document available at https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/Policy%20on%20Agency%20Accounts%20103025.pdf.

The passage comes from the Engineering Controls section of the Policy on Hazard Communication Program, but it does not describe any specific engineering controls. Instead, it notes that personal hygiene is particularly important when handling highly toxic substances and that OSHA regulations prescribe hygiene practices for certain substances. It also describes labeling, required by the Hazard Communication Regulation, as an important control measure, but only if workers read, understand, and follow label instructions. The policy stresses that compliance with labels is an essential part of worker training and that workers should know what "danger," "warning," and "caution" mean and what to do when they see them.

Under California Education Code 67380(a)(1)(A), CSULB must compile records of all occurrences reported to campus police, campus security personnel, or campus safety authorities of, and arrests for, crimes committed on campus. These are crimes involving violence, hate violence, theft, destruction of property, illegal drugs, or alcohol intoxication. The university must make this information available within two business days when students, prospective students, employees, or the media request it. To request crime information, you can contact Chief John Brockie at john.brockie@csulb.edu.

At CSULB, reassigned time and small grants for research, scholarly, and creative activity (RSCA) have generally been awarded through competitive, campus-funded programs. The best known is the Research, Scholarly, and Creative Activities (RSCA) program, sometimes described under the Scholarly and Creative Activities Awards name. It typically lets tenured and tenure-track faculty request either assigned/reassigned time (released from a course) or a modest grant or summer stipend to support a defined project. Proposals are usually reviewed first at the college level against published criteria such as merit, feasibility, and the likelihood of producing outcomes like publications, performances, or external grant applications. Recipients are generally expected to complete the work within the award period and submit a final report, which can affect eligibility for future awards. Because eligibility details, funding amounts, deadlines, and the governing Academic Senate policy number change over time, you should confirm the current rules with CSULB's Office of Research and Economic Development (or its sponsored programs office) and your college's associate dean.

I'm not sure which organization's "Policy on Volunteers" you mean, so I can't quote its specific wording or policy number. In most such policies, the "Volunteer Recruitment and Selection" section requires the organization to advertise volunteer roles openly and fairly, often with written role descriptions that outline duties, time commitments, and required skills. It usually describes a screening process, such as an application form, an interview, reference checks, and, for roles involving children or vulnerable people, background or criminal record checks. It also typically commits to non-discrimination and to matching volunteers with suitable roles, followed by orientation or training before they start. If you can share the organization's name or the text of the section, I can explain its specific provisions more precisely.

The passage doesn't state any actual rules for the "Srwc - Bldgmnt" section of the Hazard Communication Program. It appears to be a fragment of a chemical inventory listing products such as Rust-Oleum aerosol topcoat paint, Sherwin-Williams Universal Acrylic Primer, lacquer thinner, disinfectant spray, and floor cleaner. It also lists manufacturers, dates (likely for safety data sheets), and storage or use locations like "Flam Cabinet," "SRWC - Rockwall," "SRWC - General Cleaning," and the Recycling Center. To find the actual requirements, you would need the full policy document at the cited source, https://asicsulb.org/corporate/documents/discover/policies/policy-on-hazard-communication-program.pdf.

Under CSULB Policy Statement 10-10, the candidate submits the entire research, scholarly, and/or creative work section of the RTP file to the Office of Faculty Affairs, which forwards it to each external evaluator. Each evaluator is asked to report on the quality and overall impact of the candidate's submitted materials on the discipline or profession, but not to recommend on the RTP action under consideration. The AVP for Faculty Affairs tells evaluators that their reports will be included in the candidate's RTP file and that the candidate will receive a copy. Every level of review treats these reports as additional evidence, weighed alongside all other evidence in the file.

Many universities have a document titled "Policy on Master's Degrees," and you haven't said which institution's you mean, so I can't quote its specific provisions. In general, the academic load section of such a policy sets the credit or unit volume of the degree (often expressed as one to two years of full-time study), the distinction between full-time and part-time enrolment, and the minimum and maximum periods allowed for completion. It also typically explains how coursework, research, or thesis components count toward that load, and any limits on credit transfer or recognition of prior learning. If you tell me the university, I can share what I know about that institution's version, though you should check the current text with its graduate studies office or policy library.

I don't know which organization's bylaws you mean, so I can only describe how a "Special Meetings" section typically works. It covers meetings held outside the regular schedule to handle urgent or specific business. It usually says who can call one, such as the president, the board chair, a set number of directors, or a certain percentage of members. It also sets the notice requirements, often written notice a few days in advance that states the purpose, and limits the meeting to the business named in that notice. If you share the text or tell me the organization, I can explain its specific provisions.

According to ASI's Policy on Procurement, factors such as payment terms, product quality, compatibility with existing equipment, and delivery schedules can sometimes matter more than other considerations when choosing a vendor. As a recipient of federal funds, ASI is encouraged to make its best efforts to buy from "disadvantaged" businesses, including minority-owned, disabled veteran-owned, women-owned, and small businesses. ASI has local and statewide directories listing these businesses, and departments are encouraged to use them to find vendors. The ASI Business Office also purges the Supplier List annually of vendors ASI no longer does business with or chooses to avoid.

Under CSULB's Misconduct in Research & Creative Activity policy (PS 16-01), if there is a final finding of no Research Misconduct and the Respondent(s) request it, the RIO must make all reasonable and practical efforts to restore the Respondent's reputation. Depending on the circumstances and the Respondent(s)'s views, the RIO shall publicize the final outcome in any forum where the Allegation of Research Misconduct was previously publicized. Any institutional actions taken to restore the Respondent(s)'s reputation should first be approved by the DO.

Before any volunteer recruitment or assignment, a position description must be developed for each volunteer position and submitted to the Human Resources Office for review and approval. Each description must include the position's purpose and duties, a designated supervisor and worksite, a timeframe for the job, a list of qualifications, and a description of benefits. Descriptions should be reviewed and updated at least once a year, or whenever the work changes substantially. Each accepted volunteer receives the position description, which is then used in later management and evaluation, and the Human Resources Office is available to help staff develop volunteer jobs and descriptions.

I don't know which organization's "Policy on Information Systems" you mean, so I can't quote its actual User Access section. In most institutional IT policies, though, that section says who may get accounts on the organization's systems, how access is requested and approved (usually by a supervisor or data owner), and that access follows the principle of least privilege, meaning only what's needed for one's role. These sections also typically require users to keep credentials confidential, forbid sharing accounts, and call for periodic access reviews and prompt removal of access when someone changes roles or leaves. If you share the organization or the policy text, I can explain its specific provisions.

I don't know which institution's "Policy on Agency Accounts" you mean, so I can't quote its exact wording. At many universities, though, agency accounts hold money that belongs to outside or affiliated groups, such as student organizations, and the institution acts only as custodian. In those policies, the "Prohibited Use" section typically bars spending the funds on personal benefit, gifts or loans to individuals, political or lobbying activity, purchases that violate law or institutional rules (such as alcohol or illegal items), and anything outside the group's stated purpose. If you share the institution's name or paste the section, I can explain its specific provisions.

This part of the handbook appears to be a contact listing rather than a policy explanation, and "W Broadway, Long Beach, CA 90802" looks like a partial street address with no street number. It is followed by police contact information: 911 for emergencies, (562) 435-6711 for non-emergencies, and the email LBPDSexCrimes@longbeach.gov, which suggests the address belongs to the Long Beach Police Department. The passage then lists the SAFER Campus Confidential Advocate, a confidential resource staffed by Jacqueline Urtez and Rocio Telumbre, reachable at (562) 985-4770 or SAFER@csulb.edu. It ends with a heading for Student Health Services – Behavioral Health Services but gives no details for that resource.

I can't recall the exact wording or number of a CSULB policy specifically titled "authorized vendors," so I can't quote it reliably. Generally, CSULB, like other CSU campuses, requires purchases of goods and services to go through Procurement and Contract Services, and a vendor must be set up as an approved supplier in the university's financial system before it can be paid. Campus departments typically can't independently contract with or promise payment to a vendor without proper authorization. Commercial vendors who want to sell or solicit on campus usually need prior approval and must follow campus rules on time, place, and manner. For the authoritative text, check the CSULB Procurement and Contract Services website or the campus policy library, or contact that office directly.

I don't know which institution's "Policy on Student Organization Grants" you mean, so I can't tell you what its "Use of Grant Funds" section actually says. In most university policies of this kind, that section limits spending to the purposes in the approved grant application and to activities that benefit the student body, and it often requires funds to be spent within a set time frame such as the academic or fiscal year. It typically lists prohibited expenses, which commonly include alcohol, personal gifts or cash prizes, donations to other organizations, and sometimes political campaigning or travel not tied to the approved event. Many policies also require receipts or a post-event report and the return of unspent or misused funds. If you share the policy text or tell me the school, I can explain that specific section more precisely.

Under CSULB Regulation XII, students are generally individually responsible for any bodily injury, illness, or personal property loss or damage incurred while attending the University, and the University provides insurance only in specific situations. It provides medical insurance for students in NCAA team sports and obtains secondary medical insurance for registered sport club members, whose own health insurance is primary. Student travel accident insurance gives all CSU students, including those enrolled only in extended education programs, excess medical expense benefits while traveling to, from, or participating in University-sponsored activities away from campus. This accident-only coverage pays after any other health plan, excludes illness, disease, and treatment by CSU-employed or retained persons, and has a maximum benefit of $50,000 per covered person per accident.

At CSULB, student responsibility is governed mainly by the CSU Standards for Student Conduct, found in Title 5 of the California Code of Regulations, Section 41301. That code expects students to be honest, to respect the rights and safety of others, and to follow university policies. It prohibits misconduct such as cheating and plagiarism, dishonesty, disruption of university activities, harassment, alcohol or drug violations, and theft or damage of property. Violations are handled through the CSU systemwide student conduct procedures, administered on campus by Student Conduct and Ethical Development, with possible sanctions ranging from a warning to suspension or expulsion. For details or a specific situation, check the current CSULB catalog or contact that office directly, since policies are updated periodically.

As a holder of a Federalwide Assurance (FWA) filed with the federal Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP), CSULB commits that human subjects research it conducts or supports will follow the federal Common Rule (45 CFR 46) and the ethical principles of the Belmont Report. In practice, this means faculty, staff and student investigators must get review and approval or an exemption determination from the CSULB Institutional Review Board before any recruitment or data collection begins. They must also obtain informed consent as approved, and may not change approved protocols without prior IRB approval. Investigators and the institution are responsible for promptly reporting unanticipated problems involving risks to subjects or others, serious or continuing noncompliance, and suspensions or terminations of IRB approval, with the institution notifying OHRP and any funding agency as required. I don't know CSULB's exact FWA number or the specific campus policy number, so check the CSULB Office of Research and Sponsored Programs or the IRB website for the current policy text. That source would also confirm whether the campus applies these terms to all research or only to federally funded projects.

Under PS 11-06, a dean may remove a department chair without faculty consultation, but only under extraordinary circumstances. These circumstances may involve issues such as department chair confidentiality, department chair misconduct, or University liability. Before requesting the chair's resignation or removing the chair, the dean must consult with the Provost and the Associate Vice President for Faculty Affairs.

I can't quote CSULB's exact campus policy on a maximum number of major units with confidence, so I'd rather not give you a specific cap that might be wrong. What I can say is that across the CSU system, Title 5 of the California Code of Regulations sets most bachelor's degrees at 120 semester units total. Majors must also leave room for General Education and other graduation requirements, which in practice limits how large a major can be. To get the precise CSULB rule, check the "Baccalaureate Degree" or degree-requirements policy in the current CSULB Catalog or the Academic Senate policy statements, or ask your college advising center.

I can't identify the specific institution's Policy on Hazard Communication Program you mean, so I can only describe how such programs typically treat engineering controls. Hazard communication programs, modeled on OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200), generally tell employees which engineering controls protect them from the hazardous chemicals in their work area. Examples include fume hoods, local exhaust ventilation, enclosures, and process isolation. These controls are usually ranked above administrative controls and personal protective equipment in the hierarchy of controls, and Safety Data Sheets (Section 8, Exposure Controls/Personal Protection) list the appropriate engineering controls for each chemical. Your organization's own policy document or its environmental health and safety office would have the exact requirements, such as inspection or certification schedules for fume hoods.

CSULB follows the California State University systemwide nondiscrimination policy, which is now the CSU Nondiscrimination Policy and Procedures that replaced the former Executive Orders 1096 and 1097. Complaints of discrimination, harassment, sexual misconduct, dating or domestic violence, stalking, and related retaliation are handled by the campus office responsible for equity and Title IX matters. In general, that office conducts an intake and assesses the complaint, may offer supportive measures or informal resolution, and, if warranted, investigates under a "preponderance of the evidence" standard with written notice and an outcome to the parties. Exact timelines and appeal rights depend on the complaint type and the current policy version, so check with CSULB's Office of Equity & Diversity or the CSU Office of the Chancellor's website for the specifics that apply to your situation.

Although the passage is titled "Repetition of Courses (PS 23-24)," its content actually concerns the college RTP policy, and its source link points to the University RTP Policy document. It states that the college RTP policy must specify in writing the standards for evaluating candidates in all three areas of evaluation, consistent with the university RTP policy, and must ensure consistency of standards across the college. Colleges are responsible for setting standards appropriate to the breadth of their disciplines. The policy must be ratified by a majority of voting tenure-track and tenured college faculty, approved by the dean and the provost, and regularly reviewed by the college's tenure-track and tenured faculty.

Under the Policy on Facilities Use, only authorized USU/SRWC staff may be in areas where set-up, teardown, repair, or maintenance is underway, and only those staff may set up events using facility furniture and equipment. All tables and chairs must be provided by the USU/SRWC. If an event needs specific equipment the facilities don't own, reasonable accommodation will be made with prior CEO approval, but the user pays all fees for acquiring it. USU/SRWC management decides how many staff each event needs, and all groups are charged for adequate staffing and service.

I can't recall the exact wording of the fiscal reporting provision in CSU Executive Order 890, "Administration of Grants and Contracts," as applied at CSULB, so I can't quote what it says the sponsored program administrator "shall ensure." Generally, provisions like this require the administrator (at CSULB, typically the CSULB Research Foundation or the campus sponsored programs office) to make sure financial reports are accurate, complete, and submitted on time in the form the sponsor requires. They also usually require that expenditures reported are allowable, allocable, supported by documentation, and consistent with the award terms and applicable federal or state regulations. For the precise language, check the EO 890 text on the CSU Chancellor's Office website or ask CSULB's sponsored programs office.

I can't recall the specific text or number of CSULB's policy on participation in the legislative process, so I can only describe what such CSU policies generally cover. Typically, faculty, staff, and students may contact legislators and take positions on legislation as private citizens. However, they should not imply they speak for the university, and official CSULB or CSU positions are coordinated through the campus government relations office and the CSU Chancellor's Office. Employees are also generally barred from using state resources, such as work time, university email, letterhead, or equipment, for personal advocacy or political activity, consistent with California law on the use of public resources. For the exact wording and any reporting or coordination requirements, check the CSULB Policies and Procedures website or contact the university's Office of Government and Community Relations.

According to the CSULB Policies for CSULB Extension Programs, extension courses ordinarily will not be scheduled on campus. An exception is possible only where it can be clearly established that using campus facilities is essential. Even then, the extension course must not preempt or otherwise interfere with the regular instructional program. This guidance appears in the "Utilization of Campus Facilities" section of the policy, available at https://www.csulb.edu/academic-senate/policies-for-csulb-extension-programs.

Under the federal Clery Act, which applies to all California State University campuses including CSULB, the university must collect, keep, and disclose records of crimes reported on or near campus. The CSULB University Police Department maintains a daily crime log that records the nature, date, time, location, and disposition of reported crimes. The most recent 60 days of entries are open for public inspection during normal business hours, and older entries are available on request. The university also publishes an Annual Security and Fire Safety Report by October 1 each year, with three years of crime statistics and its safety policies. I don't know the specific CSULB or CSU policy number, so check the University Police website or the CSU systemwide Clery compliance policy for the exact governing document.

Under the Policy on Agency Accounts, agency funds cannot be used to open or maintain off-campus or other unauthorized bank accounts. To enforce this, checks drawn on an agency account are never made payable to the organization itself or to any of its officers. The one exception is that a check may be made payable to an officer when it reimburses legitimate, documented organization expenses.

I'm not certain what "Position Description S" refers to at CSULB. It may be a specific form version or a staff-related designation, and I don't know its exact rules. In general, CSULB requires a current position description for each staff position. The description documents the job's duties, the percentage of time spent on each, and the required qualifications, and Human Resources uses it to classify the position under CSU classification standards. At CSULB, "initiation" is mainly governed by anti-hazing rules. The CSU Student Conduct Code (Title 5, California Code of Regulations, Section 41301) prohibits hazing or conspiracy to haze in connection with initiation into, affiliation with, or continued membership in any student organization, including any act likely to cause physical harm, personal degradation, or significant psychological harm. California law also bans hazing under Education Code Sections 32050–32052 and Penal Code Section 245.6 ("Matt's Law"), and it states that the victim's consent is not a defense. Violations can bring university discipline for individuals and suspension or loss of recognition for organizations. For CSULB's exact campus wording and reporting procedures, check the Office of Student Conduct and Ethical Development or Fraternity and Sorority Life.

Under PS 19-03, reassigned time releases faculty from other duties so they can pursue research, scholarly and creative activities (RSCA), while faculty small grants are monetary awards that can cover expenses such as student assistance, minor equipment, materials and supplies, or travel. Both are awarded competitively at the college level, using support allocated by Academic Affairs that colleges may supplement with their own funds. Awards may be reassigned time, small grants, or a combination, equivalent to the Vacant Rate for up to 6 WTU per academic year, and applications for more than 3 WTU require additional justification. If more than 3 WTU of reassigned time is awarded, the awardee may take it in one semester or spread it over two. College faculty councils set the application and evaluation criteria, procedures and deadlines, determine the composition and charge of the award committee, and may establish procedures for converting reassigned time into small grants and vice versa.

In the third year, the evaluation becomes a reappointment review, and successful candidates are reappointed for one, two, or three years, followed by periodic or reappointment reviews in the fourth and fifth years as appropriate. These timelines apply to assistant professors appointed with no service credit and may vary with level of appointment and service credit.

The "Controlled Games" section explains that nonprofit organizations, including auxiliary organizations, may lawfully hold casino nights, poker nights and similar charitable fundraisers under California Business and Professions Code §19985-19987, provided both the nonprofit and any equipment or service suppliers submit an annual registration to the Bureau of Gambling Control 30 days before the event and check local police or sheriff requirements. I don't know which institution's Policy on Student Media you mean, so I can't quote its exact wording, but these sections usually follow a common pattern. Most U.S. college student media policies bar publishing material that is legally "obscene" and rely on the Supreme Court's *Miller v. California* (1973) test. Under that test, material is obscene only if it appeals to a prurient interest in sex by contemporary community standards, depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. Because of that narrow definition, such policies typically make clear that content that is merely vulgar, profane, offensive, or controversial is still protected and isn't grounds for censorship. If you share the policy text or the school's name, I can explain how its specific language applies.
